solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Jerks in bank making money (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places one thing inside another, so the jerks go inside the word for bank

blocks.note: to bank an aircraft is to tilt it, and to cock is to tilt too (cock your head)

annotation.surface: Someone at the bank cashing in on sudden jolts of the market.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' wants to be the place money lives; here it is the tilt of a plane, COCK. 'Physical jerks' is an old British phrase for gym exercises.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Russian coin worth a hundredth of a rouble, also spelt kopeck.

entries.clue: A Liberal supporting taxi group (5)

indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down clue a support holds from below, so A and L come under the taxi

annotation.surface: A Liberal politician backing a group of taxi drivers.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'supporting' means coming underneath, so the A and L follow CAB.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, narrowed: the word names a small secret group of plotters, often political.

entries.clue: Is wearing a clerical garment what could help with overseeing? (9)

indicatorNotes.wearing: clothes go round whoever wears them, so the garment goes round IS

blocks.note: a = per, as in 'ten pounds a head'
a cope is a long cloak worn by clergy
used as it stands, going inside PER COPE

annotation.surface: Asking whether dressing in vestments might help a supervisor keep watch.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: a periscope helps you see over things, 'over-seeing' rather than supervising.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: the device lets a submariner see over the waves, reading 'overseeing' as seeing over.

entries.clue: Wooden timbers said to be an essential element (4)

indicatorNotes.said: 'said' means spoken aloud, so the timbers are only heard, not spelt

blocks.note: crucks are the curved timbers framing an old building

annotation.surface: Claiming that timber is a vital ingredient of something.
annotation.walkthrough: Crucks are the paired curved beams of medieval British timber-framed houses.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the decisive point on which a matter turns.

entries.clue: Tot has to stick around to get protection (8)

indicatorNotes.around: 'around' means encircling, so the word for stick encloses the word for tot

blocks.note: to tot up is to add

annotation.surface: A small child must be kept close to be safe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a toddler but is the verb, to tot up.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an outer layer fixed to a building or pipe to shield it from weather.

entries.clue: Revolutionary chum has fits of temper and flaps (7)

indicatorNotes.Revolutionary: a revolution turns right round, so the chum is written back to front

blocks.note: a pet is a fit of sulking

annotation.surface: A radical friend who throws tantrums and panics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flaps' looks like panics to match the tantrums; it is the noun, pieces of hanging fabric. 'In a pet' is British for in a sulk.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: small hanging folds of cloth on a garment or headdress.

entries.clue: Unease of party male built up defence (10)

blocks.note: a disco is a dance party
a fort is a defence built up

annotation.surface: A man at a party grows uneasy and puts up his guard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' could be political; here it is a dance.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers mental awkwardness and anxiety as well as physical pain.

entries.clue: Diamonds linked with little country tribe once (5)

blocks.note: NI, the short form of Northern Ireland

annotation.surface: Jewels connected to a small nation's ancient people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Little' asks for an abbreviation of the country.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Once' marks a people of the past: Boudicca led this eastern English people against Rome.

entries.clue: Measuring different garden plants (9)

indicatorNotes.different: 'different' asks for the same letters in a different order

annotation.surface: Sizing up an assortment of plants in the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Measuring' reads as a verb about sizing plants up, which hides that it is exactly the letters needed.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: bright-flowered pelargoniums that fill British window boxes and borders.

entries.clue: A few words form the stage, about right (6)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means surrounding, so the stage word is put round the R

blocks.note: a stage of a process is a phase

annotation.surface: An actor's few lines spoken from the stage, more or less correctly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stage' pulls toward the theatre; it is a step in a process.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small group of words forming a unit, short of a full sentence.

entries.clue: Nasty smell with unruly part of city (7)

annotation.surface: A rundown district of town that smells.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a grim neighbourhood, and the answer sits right in it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an administrative district, as London is carved into 32 of them.

entries.clue: Former regret about famous chemist (7)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' here means turned about, facing the other way, so regret is written backwards

annotation.surface: Someone once sorry about a well-known scientist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' could mean concerning, joining regret to the chemist; it turns RUE round instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Louis, the French chemist behind pasteurisation and early vaccines.

entries.clue: Endure as a model (4)

blocks.note: first sense: to go on, hold out
second sense: a cobbler's foot-shaped wooden model

annotation.surface: Putting up with the life of a fashion model.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests the catwalk; a cobbler shapes shoes on a wooden model of a foot, and that is a last.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb of going on or holding out, and the cobbler's wooden form of a foot.

entries.clue: Scottish drink imbibed by cold couple of chaps (10)

indicatorNotes.imbibed by: what is imbibed goes inside the drinker, so the drink goes inside the letters around it

blocks.note: two men's names: DON and IAN

annotation.surface: A whisky shared by two men on a chilly day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scottish drink' reads as one phrase, whisky; 'Scottish' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Caledonia is the Roman name for Scotland, so its adjective means Scottish.

entries.clue: Unconventional, like picture removed from art gallery? (3-3-4)

annotation.definition2: like picture removed from art gallery

blocks.note: first sense: the idiom for bizarre, eccentric

blocks.clueFragment: like picture removed from art gallery
blocks.note: second sense: taken down from where it hung, read literally

annotation.surface: A quirky artwork taken down in a gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads the idiom literally, which the question mark flags.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the idiom for eccentric, and read literally, a picture taken down from its hook.

entries.clue: Indifference shown by a nincompoop turning head (9)

indicatorNotes.turning: 'turning' means turning round, so the nincompoop is written backwards

blocks.note: a ness is a headland, as in place names like Sheerness

annotation.surface: A fool who turns their head away, showing they couldn't care less.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turning head' reads as a gesture; 'turning' reverses the fool, and 'head' is a headland.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: keeping coolly apart from things is a kind of indifference.

entries.clue: Bill departed, as a man found innocent (9)

blocks.note: to quit a place is to depart it

annotation.surface: A man cleared in court walks out of the dock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, fitting the courtroom; it is an account, AC.
annotation.definitionFit: A verdict clearing a man leaves him legally innocent; the participle describes him.

entries.clue: Ballet position found to be tricky (5)

indicatorNotes.tricky: something tricky is hard to pin down, a hint the letters must be worked into a new order

annotation.surface: A dancer finds a ballet pose difficult.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the verb of the sentence; it is only the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A ballet term: a movement lowering the body by bending the supporting leg.

entries.clue: No sailor dies at sea? That’s officially confirmed (9)

indicatorNotes.at sea: to be at sea is to be confused, so the letters of dies are jumbled

annotation.surface: An official record that no sailor died on the voyage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' sits naturally with a sailor, but it means muddled.
annotation.definitionFit: A document certified by a notary public has been officially attested.

entries.clue: What French saint is seen in pursuit? (5)

annotation.surface: Asking which French saint appears in a chase.
annotation.walkthrough: The question reads as a trivia puzzle; 'What French' is the French word for 'what'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a long search for something, as knights went on for the Grail.

entries.clue: Curbs ways to limit speed (9)

indicatorNotes.to limit: to limit is to form the boundary, so the ways word forms the edges round the speed

blocks.note: modes are ways of doing things

annotation.surface: Road measures that slow the traffic down.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all traffic calming; 'Curbs' is a verb, not the kerb at the roadside.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to restrain or temper something, as a curb on a horse does.

entries.clue: Maybe harmful chemical upset stomach — a fellow taken short (7)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue 'upset' means turned upside down, so the stomach word is written bottom to top
indicatorNotes.taken short: 'short' means cut short, so the fellow loses his last letter

annotation.surface: A man caught short with an upset stomach from something toxic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset stomach' reads as illness; 'taken short' is British slang for urgently needing a toilet, here just a shortened word.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an agent causing genetic mutation, and 'maybe' admits not all are harmful.

entries.clue: Blunt little female minister putting men off (6)

indicatorNotes.putting: 'putting … off' is one instruction, to put the men off, so they are removed from the minister
indicatorNotes.off: 'off' means removed, so the men come off the minister

blocks.note: a rector is a parish minister
OR = other ranks, the enlisted men; removed

annotation.surface: A small woman vicar is so outspoken she drives men away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Men' is the military OR, other ranks, which comes out of RECTOR.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: straight-talking and frank, the way a blunt remark is.

entries.clue: Home crowd at match — in need of a time for police officers? (10)

indicatorNotes.in need of: to be in need of something is to lack it, so a time is missing from the crowd

blocks.note: the crowd at a match are spectators
A plus T = time; both removed

annotation.surface: A home crowd waiting for the police to arrive in time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In need of' means lacking: the spectators are missing A and T.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the rank above sergeant in British police forces.

entries.clue: Second eleven? It may be let off when there is bad language (5)

annotation.definition: It may be let off when there is bad language

blocks.note: an eleven is a team, in cricket or football

annotation.surface: A reserve team swearing while blowing off their frustration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second eleven' reads as the reserve side, one phrase; it splits into S and TEAM.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: swearing is one way to let off steam, releasing pent-up anger.

entries.clue: Catch some retreating (4)

indicatorNotes.retreating: a retreating army goes backwards, so the word for some is written backwards

annotation.surface: Capturing some of an army in retreat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Some retreating' reads as fleeing troops; it is PART going backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to snare an animal or a suspect is to catch it.

entries.clue: Pain associated with a knife (5)

blocks.note: a pang is a sharp pain

annotation.surface: Pain caused by a blade.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface links pain to a knife wound, and the answer is in the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a broad-bladed East African machete.

entries.clue: Husband in club making a bit of money (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places one thing inside another, so the husband goes inside the club

annotation.surface: A husband earning a little at his club.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a social club; it is a bat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the unit of Thai currency.

entries.clue: Exotic seafood’s strong taste acquiring reputation (7)

indicatorNotes.acquiring: to acquire is to take in, so the taste takes the reputation inside it

blocks.note: a tang is a sharp taste

annotation.surface: A foreign delicacy whose strong flavour is making a name for itself.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive but stands for 'has', joining the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: sea cucumber, dried and eaten as a delicacy in East Asian cooking.

entries.clue: Song in church, a new song endlessly going on (7)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: without its end, so the second song loses its final letter

annotation.surface: A new hymn in church that drags on forever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Song in church' looks like one idea, a hymn; 'Song' alone is the definition, and the setter reuses the word in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowing: the French word for song, used in English for a French cabaret or art song.

entries.clue: Get rid of fish stew component? (8)

blocks.note: to dump is to get rid of

annotation.surface: Throwing out an ingredient of a fish stew.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fish stew' reads as one dish; 'fish' belongs to the wordplay and 'stew component' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a ball of suet dough traditionally simmered in a British stew.

entries.clue: Arenas remain expensive, as some might say? (6)

indicatorNotes.as some might say: what some might say is spoken, so the phrase is heard, not spelt

annotation.surface: Complaining that sports grounds are still costly.
annotation.walkthrough: Dear means expensive in British usage; 'some' covers accents where the match is close.
annotation.definitionFit: The Latin-style plural of stadium; stadiums are sports arenas.
